start.hint: Luna's owner is worried because the cat is straining to urinate and there's blood in the urine. In cats this could be bacterial UTI, idiopathic FLUTD, or even a urethral obstruction (dangerous in males, rarer in females). Your first step is to take a complete history from the owner — how long, what symptoms, diet, and any prior episodes. Then examine Luna.
start.text:
CASE BRIEF
Luna — 5F (spayed) domestic shorthair cat, 4.2 kg


CHECK-IN COMPLAINT
Mrs. Chen presents Luna at your veterinary clinic. She explains: 'Luna has been going in and out of her litter box all night but barely producing anything — and I can see blood in the little bit she does pass. She cried out twice when she tried to go. This started two days ago.'


INITIAL ASSESSMENT
HR 185 bpm | BP 128/84 | RR 26 | Temp 39.4°C | SpO₂ 99% | Pain 2/10

• Luna is alert and responsive, mildly tense when you handle her
• Mucous membranes pink and moist; CRT < 2 seconds
• Coat is well-groomed; body condition score 4/9 (lean-normal)
• Mild pain response on caudal abdominal palpation


OWNER OBSERVATIONS
• Blood-tinged urine in litter box × 2 days
• Frequent trips to box with minimal output (stranguria / pollakiuria)
• Crying out occasionally during attempts to urinate
• Appetite reduced since yesterday
• No vomiting, no diarrhoea

─────────────────────────────────────────────
CLINICAL IMPRESSION
A 5-year-old spayed female cat presenting with haematuria, stranguria, and pollakiuria × 2 days. Top differentials: bacterial UTI, idiopathic feline lower urinary tract disease (iFLUTD), urolithiasis. Urethral obstruction is less common in females but must be considered. Collect history, perform physical examination, then run a urinalysis on a cystocentesis sample.

choices.text: Take a complete history from Mrs. Chen — duration, symptoms, diet, environment
Begin physical examination immediately — worry about history later

effects.reason: Skipping the owner history misses key context — duration, diet, prior episodes, and home environment all influence your differential and management

choices.text: Order a urinalysis immediately — the signs are obvious enough

effects.reason: Ordering tests without a history or physical exam skips important diagnostic steps — you may miss concurrent findings or choose the wrong tests

history-hub.hint: Cover the key areas: urinary symptoms (the main complaint), diet and water intake (important risk factors for FLUTD and UTI), living environment and stress (idiopathic FLUTD is often stress-triggered), and past medical history. Once you have enough, proceed to the physical examination.
history-hub.text:
Mrs. Chen is attentive and cooperative. You need a focused history.

What aspects do you want to explore?

choices.text: Urinary symptoms — frequency, straining, blood, pain, output volume
Diet and water intake — food type, fluid consumption, any recent changes
Living environment — indoor/outdoor, litter box setup, recent stressors
Past medical history — prior UTIs, vaccinations, medications
I have enough history — proceed to physical examination

history-urinary.text:
Mrs. Chen describes Luna's urinary symptoms in detail:

• Started 2 days ago — Luna began visiting the litter box much more frequently than usual
• She sits in the box, strains, and produces only a few drops each time (pollakiuria + stranguria)
• The urine is blood-tinged — Mrs. Chen noticed pink-red spots in the clay litter
• Luna has cried out twice during attempts to urinate — audible vocalisation suggesting pain
• She has not gone 'normally' since this started
• No evidence of urinating anywhere other than the litter box (no periuria noted)
• No blood seen near the vulva between attempts (no continuous haemorrhage)

The combination of haematuria + stranguria + pollakiuria in an intact/spayed female cat has a broad differential, but bacterial UTI with cystitis is a strong candidate. Idiopathic FLUTD (Pandora syndrome) is also possible — it is actually more common in cats overall, but less likely in a 5-year-old with a confirmed fever.

choices.text: Continue taking history

history-diet-water.text:
Diet and water intake:

• Luna eats exclusively dry kibble (no wet food) — Mrs. Chen has never offered wet food
• Water intake: Mrs. Chen provides a single ceramic bowl of still water. She estimates Luna drinks 'a normal amount' but admits she's never closely monitored it
• No dietary changes in the past month
• No treats other than occasional dry kibble pieces

Clinical relevance — IMPORTANT:
Dry-food-only diets are a well-established risk factor for feline lower urinary tract disease. Cats evolved as desert predators and get most of their hydration from prey (roughly 70% water). Dry kibble contains only 10–12% moisture. Chronically low water intake produces concentrated urine (high specific gravity) — which predisposes to UTI, crystal formation, and idiopathic FLUTD.

Recommending increased wet food and a water fountain will be an important part of Luna's discharge advice.

choices.text: Continue taking history

history-environment.text:
Living environment and potential stressors:

• Luna is strictly indoor — never goes outside
• Single-cat household
• One litter box (scooped daily, changed weekly)
• Recent changes: Mrs. Chen's adult son moved in approximately 3 weeks ago — new person in the household, some rearranging of furniture, occasional loud music late at night
• Luna has been hiding under the bed more than usual since the son arrived

Clinical context:
Environmental stress is the primary trigger for idiopathic FLUTD (iFLUTD) in cats. A new person, changed layout, and disrupted routine all represent significant stressors for a cat. However, iFLUTD typically self-resolves within 3–7 days and does not cause fever — Luna's temperature of 39.4°C suggests an infectious or inflammatory process beyond pure iFLUTD. Bacterial UTI, potentially superimposed on stress-related FLUTD, remains the leading diagnosis.

choices.text: Continue taking history

history-pmhx.text:
Past medical history:

• Spayed at 6 months of age — no complications
• Vaccinations: up to date (FVRCP + Rabies — last updated 10 months ago)
• No prior urinary episodes — this is the first time
• No known drug allergies
• No prior illnesses or hospitalisations
• No medications currently
• Annual wellness exams — last exam 10 months ago; all normal at that time

Note: Being a first episode with fever and positive urine findings raises the suspicion of a true bacterial UTI rather than idiopathic FLUTD. Cats with iFLUTD typically have recurrent episodes and no fever.

effects.reason: Complete history obtained from owner — covers urinary signs, diet risk factors, environment, and past medical history

choices.text: Good — proceed to physical examination

examination-hub.hint: In a cat presenting with urinary signs, your exam priorities are: (1) abdominal palpation — is the bladder distended or painful? Can you express urine? (2) Check for signs of systemic illness — dehydration, lymphadenopathy. A blocked urethra is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate relief, but that is more common in male cats. Luna is female, so obstruction is less likely but worth ruling out with palpation.
examination-hub.text:
You prepare to examine Luna. She is sitting on the exam table, alert but tense.

What aspects of the physical exam do you focus on?

choices.text: Palpate the abdomen — assess bladder size, pain, and check for urethral obstruction
General assessment — dehydration, lymph nodes, pain score, mucous membranes
Examination complete — proceed to investigations

exam-abdominal.text:
You gently palpate Luna's abdomen.

• Bladder: Small and firm, located in the caudal abdomen. Mild pain response — Luna tenses and vocalises softly when you palpate the bladder. A small amount of urine is present. The bladder wall feels slightly thickened.
• Urethra: No firm, cord-like obstruction palpable in the perineal region. Luna was able to produce a few drops during check-in, confirming the urethra is patent.
• Kidneys: Normal size bilaterally, smooth contour, non-painful on palpation — no evidence of nephromegaly or renomegaly suggesting upper tract involvement.
• No palpable abdominal masses, no mesenteric lymphadenopathy.
• No peritoneal signs.

Findings: Small, mildly painful bladder with wall thickening. Urethra patent. Kidneys normal. No obstruction. These findings are consistent with cystitis — the bladder itself is inflamed.

effects.reason: Physical examination performed — bladder palpated, urethra patent, kidneys assessed. No obstruction identified.

choices.text: Continue examination

exam-general.text:
General physical assessment:

• Hydration: Skin tent recoil normal, mucous membranes moist — adequately hydrated.
• Lymph nodes: Submandibular and popliteal lymph nodes non-enlarged, non-painful.
• Coat: Well-groomed overall; no overgrooming of the perineal or caudal abdominal region.
• Eyes / Nasal: No discharge, no respiratory distress.
• Temperature: 39.4°C confirmed (normal feline range 38.0–39.2°C) — mild pyrexia consistent with active infection.
• Heart and lungs: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmur. Clear lung fields.
• Pain score: 2/10 — Luna shows mild intermittent discomfort during caudal palpation, consistent with a moderate perceived pain level (cats suppress pain responses).

Note: Cats are experts at masking pain. A pain score of 2/10 in this context likely represents a clinically meaningful level of discomfort.

choices.text: Continue examination

investigation-hub.hint: The single most important test here is a urinalysis on a cystocentesis sample. Cystocentesis (a sterile needle aspirate from the bladder) gives you an uncontaminated sample — unlike free-catch, which can be contaminated by vulvar bacteria. From the sample you can run a dipstick + sediment exam in-house in 10 minutes. Also send a urine culture for antimicrobial stewardship. CBC and chemistry add context. Ultrasound rules out stones.
investigation-hub.text:
Physical examination suggests cystitis. Your working differential:
1. Bacterial UTI (most likely — fever, first episode, positive palpation findings)
2. Idiopathic FLUTD (possible — environmental stress, dry diet)
3. Urolithiasis (possible — collect urine, consider ultrasound)

What investigations do you want to run?

choices.text: Collect urine via cystocentesis (sterile bladder tap) — gold standard sample
Run urinalysis (dipstick + sediment exam) on collected sample
Send urine for culture & sensitivity (antimicrobial stewardship)
Order CBC and chemistry panel — check for systemic effects
Order abdominal ultrasound — rule out urolithiasis (stones)
I have enough information — proceed to treatment

urine-collection-result.text:
You prepare the cystocentesis.

With Luna in lateral recumbency, you clip a small area of caudal ventral abdomen, prep with alcohol, and use a 22G needle attached to a 6 mL syringe. Under palpation guidance, you aspirate the bladder.

• 3 mL of amber, cloudy urine obtained — good sample
• Luna tolerates the procedure well with minimal restraint
• The cloudiness and colour are already notable — clear, pale-yellow urine is normal in cats

Cystocentesis advantages:
• Sterile sample — eliminates contamination from the urethra, vulva, and prepuce
• Gold standard for urine culture interpretation
• Quick, safe, and well-tolerated in most cats

The sample is ready for urinalysis and culture.

effects.reason: Urine sample collected via cystocentesis — sterile technique, gold standard for culture interpretation

choices.text: Run the urinalysis on this sample

urinalysis-result.hint: The UA is abnormal — high WBCs, bacteria, blood, and high specific gravity. This pattern (pyuria + bacteriuria + haematuria) is the hallmark of bacterial UTI in cats. The high SG (1.042) tells you the kidneys are concentrating urine well — no renal insufficiency. Send this sample for culture before starting antibiotics so you can target therapy.
urinalysis-result.text:
URINALYSIS RESULTS (cystocentesis sample)

Macroscopic:
• Colour: Amber
• Turbidity: Cloudy
• Specific gravity: 1.042 (concentrated — normal ≥1.035 for cats)

Dipstick:
• Leukocyte esterase: 3+
• Nitrites: Positive
• Blood: 3+
• Protein: 1+
• pH: 6.5

Sediment exam (400× microscopy):
• WBCs: 42/hpf (normal 0–5/hpf)
• RBCs: 18/hpf (normal 0–5/hpf)
• Bacteria: Many rod-shaped organisms
• No casts, no crystals

INTERPRETATION
The findings are diagnostic of bacterial cystitis:
• Pyuria (42 WBCs/hpf) — white cells in the bladder = inflammation/infection
• Bacteriuria — rod-shaped organisms (likely E. coli or Pasteurella)
• Haematuria — bleeding from inflamed mucosa
• High specific gravity — kidneys are concentrating normally; no renal involvement at this stage
• Absence of crystals — makes struvite or oxalate urolithiasis less likely, though ultrasound can confirm

DIAGNOSIS CONFIRMED: Bacterial Urinary Tract Infection (Cystitis)

effects.reason: Urinalysis performed — pyuria, bacteriuria, and haematuria confirmed. Bacterial UTI diagnosis established.

choices.text: Order a urine culture before starting antibiotics, then proceed to treatment
Diagnosis clear — proceed directly to treatment

urine-culture-result.text:
Urine culture submitted.

You submit the cystocentesis sample to the laboratory for aerobic culture and sensitivity testing.

Preliminary report: Cloudy urine. Gram-negative rods on direct smear.
Full culture with sensitivity results: 3–5 days (will be available for follow-up visit)

Why this matters:
• Culture-directed therapy is the standard of care for UTI
• It identifies the causative organism and its antibiotic sensitivities
• It allows de-escalation or adjustment if empiric therapy fails
• It reduces unnecessary use of broad-spectrum antibiotics (antimicrobial stewardship)

You will start empiric antibiotics based on common uropathogens in cats. Amoxicillin-clavulanate and trimethoprim-sulfa are first-line choices for feline UTI — both have good gram-negative and gram-positive coverage with low resistance rates in community-acquired cat UTI.

effects.reason: Urine culture & sensitivity ordered — enables targeted therapy and supports antimicrobial stewardship

choices.text: Culture sent — now choose empiric antibiotic treatment

cbc-chemistry-result.text:
BLOODWORK RESULTS

CBC:
• WBC: 14.2 × 10³/µL (ref 5.5–19.5) — mild leukocytosis
• Neutrophils: 10.8 × 10³/µL — neutrophilia (active infection marker)
• Haematocrit: 35% (ref 30–45%) — low-normal
• Platelets: Normal

Chemistry Panel:
• BUN: 28 mg/dL (ref 14–36) — normal
• Creatinine: 1.2 mg/dL (ref 0.6–2.4) — normal
• ALT: 45 U/L — normal
• Glucose: 118 mg/dL — mildly elevated (likely stress hyperglycaemia)

INTERPRETATION
Mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia — consistent with active bacterial infection. Renal function is intact (BUN and creatinine normal) — no evidence of pyelonephritis or upper tract involvement at this stage. The mildly elevated glucose in a stressed cat in clinic is a common and expected finding — not concerning for diabetes.

Bloodwork supports a localised lower urinary tract infection without systemic complications.

choices.text: Continue investigations

ultrasound-result.text:
ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND

Bladder:
• Wall thickening: 3.5 mm (normal < 1.7 mm) — consistent with cystitis
• Bladder contents: Increased echogenicity (cellular debris / pus / blood)
• Uroliths (stones): None identified
• Urethra: Patent — no obstruction

Kidneys:
• Bilateral normal size and echogenicity
• No renal pelvis dilation (rules out hydronephrosis or upper tract obstruction)
• No pyelonephritis changes

Other: No free abdominal fluid. No other masses.

INTERPRETATION
Ultrasound confirms cystitis (thickened bladder wall, echogenic contents) WITHOUT urolithiasis or urethral obstruction. This is reassuring — no stones means antimicrobial therapy alone should be sufficient. Upper tract is normal — infection appears confined to the lower urinary tract.

choices.text: Good — continue investigations or proceed to treatment

treatment-hub.hint: First-line antibiotics for feline UTI are amoxicillin-clavulanate (Clavamox — 62.5 mg PO BID × 10–14 days) or trimethoprim-sulfa (15 mg/kg PO BID × 10–14 days). Both provide excellent gram-negative and gram-positive coverage. Fluoroquinolones (like enrofloxacin) should be reserved for culture-confirmed resistant cases — using them first-line depletes your last-resort drugs and risks retinal toxicity in cats at high doses. After prescribing, educate Mrs. Chen on wet food, a water fountain to increase hydration, and return in 7 days.
treatment-hub.text:

Choose your treatment approach:

outcome-excellent.text:
Luna is discharged with a treatment plan.

Treatment summary:
• Antibiotic: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 62.5 mg PO BID × 14 days (or TMS 15 mg/kg BID × 14 days)
• Wet food transition: Introduce a quality wet food to increase dietary moisture
• Water fountain: Switch to a recirculating water fountain to encourage drinking
• Activity: Encourage play and environmental enrichment to reduce stress (new housemate adjustment)
• Recheck: Return in 7 days for re-examination and to review culture results
• Owner education: Signs of recurrence — straining, blood, vocalising when urinating

Clinical course (follow-up notes):
Day 3: Mrs. Chen calls — Luna is urinating normally again, no blood visible. Eating better.
Day 7 (recheck): Luna bright and alert. No urinary signs. Bladder non-painful on palpation. Repeat UA: WBC 2/hpf, no bacteria — infection resolved.
Culture result (day 5): E. coli, sensitive to amoxicillin-clavulanate and TMS. Antibiotic choice confirmed appropriate.
Day 14: Course completed. Luna doing well. Mrs. Chen has switched to a mixed wet/dry diet and set up a water fountain.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Excellent work. This was a thorough approach to feline lower urinary tract disease:

✓ Complete history from owner — identified dry-diet risk factor and environmental stress trigger
✓ Physical examination — bladder palpated, urethra confirmed patent
✓ Cystocentesis — sterile urine sample, gold standard collection technique
✓ Urinalysis — pyuria, bacteriuria, and haematuria confirmed bacterial UTI
✓ Urine culture — enables targeted therapy and antimicrobial stewardship
✓ First-line antibiotic — appropriate agent, correct duration
✓ Owner education — dietary changes and recheck planned

Key teaching points:
• Cats on dry-food-only diets produce highly concentrated urine which predisposes to UTI and FLUTD
• A fever in a cat with lower urinary signs raises the probability of true bacterial UTI over idiopathic FLUTD
• Cystocentesis is superior to free-catch for culture accuracy
• Fluoroquinolones should be reserved for culture-confirmed resistant infections in cats — not first-line
• A urine culture at recheck (post-treatment) confirms cure

outcome-fluoroquinolone.text:
Luna is discharged with enrofloxacin.

Clinical outcome: Luna does improve — enrofloxacin is bactericidal for most gram-negative uropathogens. Her urinary signs resolve by day 4.

However, your pharmacist contacts you the following day after reviewing the prescription, and your attending veterinarian raises a concern at morning rounds.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Enrofloxacin is effective against most gram-negative uropathogens (including E. coli) and the patient improved — but this was not the right first-line choice.

WHY FLUOROQUINOLONES SHOULD NOT BE FIRST-LINE IN CATS:

1. Retinal toxicity risk:
   Enrofloxacin is uniquely toxic to the feline retinal tapetal layer at elevated or prolonged doses. This causes sudden-onset irreversible blindness. The risk is dose-dependent — 5 mg/kg SID is the maximum safe dose for cats. The risk is real and well-documented; many practitioners have seen it.

2. Antimicrobial stewardship:
   Fluoroquinolones are 'reserve' antibiotics in veterinary medicine. First-line feline UTI is caused predominantly by E. coli and Staphylococcus — organisms that respond well to amoxicillin-clavulanate and TMS. Using fluoroquinolones empirically without culture evidence of resistance depletes your last-resort drugs and drives resistance.

3. Better choices were available:
   • Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Clavamox): First-line, well-tolerated, excellent UTI penetration
   • Trimethoprim-sulfa: Well-absorbed into urine, cost-effective

Key lesson: Save fluoroquinolones for culture-confirmed resistant infections where first-line antibiotics have failed.

outcome-no-treatment.text:
Luna is sent home without antibiotics.

Mrs. Chen calls 3 days later. Luna is worse — she has not eaten in 2 days, is hiding under the bed, and is now producing only a drop of very dark urine. She appears lethargic.

On emergency re-presentation:
• HR 210 bpm | RR 32 | Temp 40.1°C | Pain: 5/10
• Luna is moderately dehydrated — skin tent, tacky mucous membranes
• Kidney values: BUN 58, Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL — acute kidney injury developing
• UA repeat: 80+ WBCs/hpf, heavy bacteriuria, glucose in urine (stress/renal)

Luna is hospitalised for 3 days: IV fluids, IV amoxicillin-clavulanate, pain management.

─────────────────────────────────────────────
DEBRIEF

Waiting for culture results before starting antibiotics is NOT appropriate when:
• The diagnosis of bacterial UTI is already confirmed on urinalysis (pyuria + bacteriuria + haematuria)
• The patient has a fever and is clearly uncomfortable

Culture results take 3–5 days. Sending a cat home with confirmed bacterial cystitis and no treatment allows the infection to ascend to the kidneys (pyelonephritis) and cause systemic illness.

The correct approach:
→ Run the urinalysis first (quick, in-house, 10 minutes)
→ Confirm bacterial infection
→ Start empiric antibiotics immediately based on likely organisms
→ Use culture results at recheck to confirm sensitivities and adjust if needed

Culture should guide therapy — not delay it.
